doc.title: Fred Lipsius interviewed by Monk Rowe. Boston, Massachusetts, July 25, 2018

title: Impact of the Lonesome Suzie arrangement
summary: Rowe says the horn parts affected him; Lipsius describes the build, Dick Halligan's baritone horn, and Bob Mann's praise.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Session players on the hits: "I played on that record"

blocks.x: I’m telling you, some of that music, those horn parts and stuff just made a profound effect on me. And sometimes it was those dissonances that resolve, and I would go to the piano and go what is that. And so I just wanted to, as I said early on I’ve been waiting to talk to you since 1969 so I could say that.

No but as you just started to talk I almost start to feel like crying because it reminded me, maybe, of when I was in the studio and we finally heard it back, I’ve felt this with a couple of my arrangements. This is just me. I’m a sensitive person. Sometimes I don’t like being so sensitive. I’m not always. But I almost cried listening to my arrangement because it’s very powerful. It starts out with a whisper, there is nothing, just him and a bass. And it builds. And the middle part where it starts to make the transition, we rented a baritone horn, which was the original horn that Dick Halligan played — Dick Halligan wrote, I was just reading his book called Musical Being. It’s a book about his life. Very good. He has all the details about his life. But he says his first instrument is baritone horn. So in the middle, to make the transition, he goes [scats] if you remember that. And then it opens up and then the horns play that thing [scats] later on. But it just builds and I’m almost in tears. And our manager, who was Steve Katz, Steve Katz was a guitar player, his brother was our manager or lawyer, not manager, lawyer. And he came in to hear us and he says, “Who’s singing?” Because David’s very guttural. But he’s going [scats] like Artie Garfunkel almost. You know? And he changes his voice. It’s like how many singers can do that? Singing up high, right in pitch, and then it’s really ballsy later on. So but the whole chart, it was like there is nothing like that. And I remember Bob Mann, who’s dad used to be the piano player or something on the Arthur Godfrey Show, Bob Mann played with everybody. Well Taylor, James Taylor. He was with him for years. Perfect pitch. And he asked me one day, again I’m not bragging but he said, “Who did that arrangement of ‘Lonesome Suzie?’” I said, “I did.” You know because it’s so different. Like “Spinning Wheel” too. That’s what, and people say where’s the big band thing? I say, “I listen to Benny Goodman.” Dick Halligan listened to the Hi-Lo’s, Stan Kenton, all these people. So it’s natural, and like I’m also I heard on the first one in the rock & roll books that played bebop and rock & roll on their alto solos. The first horn player to do that. I didn’t look in the book but that’s what I do. For the last twenty years I hear a little Coltrane all of a sudden I’m growling, because I heard that. I used to hear rock & roll as a kid. It’s not contrived, and then you hear all these other players doing stuff, whatever.
